scenes.say: Every object is born by a constructor and dies by a destructor. Soon you'll explain move semantics in one picture. And why s t d move doesn't move anything.
Interviewers hand you a class that prints in every constructor. Today you trace its births and deaths. Then you see a move steal instead of copy. Then references and forwarding decide which one runs.
lines: See a move steal instead of copy

scenes.title: What does this print?
scenes.statement: A class prints a word in every constructor and in its destructor. Predict the full output for three objects.

example.input: T a; T b(7); T c = b;
example.output: default param7 copy7 dtor7 dtor7 dtor0

scenes.say: Can you trace a class that talks? For example, three objects: a, b with seven, c copied from b. Six words come out.

scenes.head: Three ways to be born
scenes.say: Think of ordering coffee. A plain coffee is the default constructor. Your own order is parameterized. And same as his is the copy constructor.

scenes.head: Trace the three births
scenes.say: Here is the class. Each constructor prints its name. A is plain, so default. B passes seven, so param seven. C copies b, so copy seven. Then they die in reverse: c, b, a.

output.text: default param7 copy7 dtor7 dtor7 dtor0

scenes.say: Your turn. Add a fourth object, d, made plain. Then assign d equals c. How many times does copy print in total? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: After `T b(7); T c = b; T d; d = c;`, how many `copy` words print?

scenes.head: Copy constructor or assignment?
scenes.say: It's one. Only c equals b builds a new object. Passing b by value copies into the parameter too. But d equals c, with d alive, is assignment, and prints nothing. Declare any constructor, and the plain one is gone. A copy constructor takes a reference, or it would copy forever.

scenes.title: When does each object die?
scenes.statement: A class prints plus when built and minus when destroyed. Predict the output for a local, an inner scope and a heap object.

example.input: T a; { T b; } T* h = new T; delete h;

scenes.say: Who dies first? For example, a local a, an inner scope with b, and a heap object h. In what order?

scenes.head: Last built, first destroyed
scenes.say: Think of a stack of plates: last on, first off. A is built, plus a. B is built inside its braces. The brace closes, and b dies first. Now h is built on the heap. It dies only at delete. Finally main ends, and a dies.

scenes.head: The same program, with output
scenes.say: Same program, inside main. The constructor prints plus, the destructor prints minus. Plus a, plus b. The closing brace gives minus b. Plus h, and delete gives minus h. Then main ends: minus a.
Your turn. Three locals in one scope: a, then b, then c. In what order do they die? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Scope holds T a, T b, T c, in that order. Destroyed in?

scenes.head: When each kind of object dies
scenes.say: It's c, b, a. Last built, first destroyed. A local dies at its closing brace. A heap object, only at delete. A temporary, at its semicolon. Globals, after main returns. An exception unwinds the locals. Inside one object: body, members reversed, then base.

scenes.head: Why no virtual constructor?
scenes.say: Can a constructor be virtual? No: G C C says constructors cannot be declared virtual. Virtual calls use a hidden v pointer in the object. Derived is built in layers, base first. While Base runs, the v pointer points at the Base table, so hello prints Base. Then Derived starts, and the pointer switches.

scenes.head: Want one anyway? Clone
scenes.say: Need the effect? Write an ordinary virtual function that constructs. Each class overrides clone, calling its own copy constructor. Copy any shape through a base reference, and you get the right type. Destructors, unlike constructors, should be virtual.

scenes.title: Push a megabyte string
scenes.statement: A vector of strings receives one string holding a megabyte of text. Get it in without duplicating the megabyte.

example.input: one 1 MB string into a vector

scenes.say: Picture a vector of strings, and a string holding a megabyte. For example, we push it in. Copying makes a second megabyte. We want none.

scenes.head: Copy duplicates, move hands over keys
scenes.say: Think of moving house. Copying builds a second house and carries everything over. Moving hands over the keys. Here, a points to a one megabyte block. A move copies the pointer and size to b. Then a becomes null, so only b owns the block.

scenes.head: What std::move really does
scenes.say: So what does s t d move do? Take your variable s. Wrap it: one cast to an rvalue reference, and no code runs. Overload resolution now picks the move constructor. And the move constructor steals the buffer.

scenes.head: A move constructor
scenes.say: A move constructor takes an rvalue reference, two ampersands. It binds only to things about to be discarded. We copy the pointer and size, then empty the source. Mark it noexcept, or vector copies when it grows. A thousand ints moved, and a is empty.
Your turn. A constant string k, and we write t equals s t d move of k. Does anything get stolen? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `const string k = ...; string t = std::move(k);` What runs?

scenes.head: Three traps
scenes.say: A copy. A constant can't be stolen from, so it silently copies. Trap two: return s t d move of a local. It blocks building in place, and G C C warns. Just return s. Trap three: after a move, the value is unspecified.

chapters.title: Is it a house or a pizza?

scenes.title: Can I take its address?
scenes.statement: Every expression has a category. It says whether you may take its address, assign to it, or steal from it.

example.output: only x has a lasting address

scenes.say: Every expression has a category. Which of these has an address? For example, x, five, and x plus one. Only x.

scenes.head: A house and a pizza
scenes.say: Think of a house and a pizza delivery. A house has an address and stays put: an lvalue, like x. A pizza in the bag has no address: an rvalue, like x plus one. S t d move makes an xvalue: a house treated as the pizza.

scenes.head: What references can bind to
scenes.say: References pick sides. An lvalue reference, one ampersand, binds only lvalues. A const reference binds anything. An rvalue reference, two ampersands, binds only rvalues. Nobody else can see a temporary, so it's safe to steal. And s t d move turns x into an rvalue.
Your turn. Inside take, s has type rvalue reference to string. We write string a equals s. Copy or move? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `void take(string&& s)` runs `string a = s;`. Copy or move?

scenes.head: A named rvalue reference is an lvalue
scenes.say: Copy. The type of s is an rvalue reference. But the expression s has a name, so it's an lvalue. Type and category are different things. To move, say s t d move again.

scenes.title: Pass it on unchanged
scenes.statement: A wrapper hands its argument to another function. A named object must arrive as a copy, a temporary as a move.
scenes.say: A wrapper hands its argument on. For example, wrap of a named t, then wrap of a temporary. What should arrive? Copy first, then move.

scenes.head: The wrapper loses the rvalue
scenes.say: Two overloads of take. One copies, one moves. The wrapper passes its argument along. A named t copies, correct. But a temporary should move, and it prints copy again. Inside the wrapper, a has a name, so it's an lvalue.

scenes.head: How X remembers
scenes.say: How does X remember? Pass the named t: X is deduced as T ampersand. The ampersands collapse to one, so forward keeps an lvalue: copy. Pass a temporary: X is plain T, and forward casts back to an rvalue: move.

scenes.head: The fix: std::forward
scenes.say: Two ingredients. First, a parameter X and and, with X deduced: a forwarding reference. It accepts anything. Second, s t d forward of X. It casts back to an rvalue only if one came in. Now it prints copy, then move.
Your turn. Same wrapper, with forward. We call wrap with s t d move of t. What prints? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Where it's used, and the traps
scenes.say: Move: the argument is an rvalue, so forward casts. This is how make unique and emplace back pass arguments on. Trap: only X and and with X deduced is a forwarding reference. A vector of int and and is not. Forward each argument once.

scenes.title: How many constructors?
scenes.statement: A function returns an object by value. Count how many constructor calls the compiler really makes.

example.input: T a = make(); T b = named();

scenes.say: Return an object by value: how much work is that? For example, make and named, one temporary, one local. Only two constructors.

scenes.head: Count the constructor calls
scenes.say: T announces every constructor. Make returns a temporary. Named returns a local variable. Naively each could build an object, then copy or move it out. But the output is just ctor, ctor. Both calls were elided.

scenes.head: NRVO: build it where it ends up
scenes.say: Naively, t is built inside named, then moved out into b. With N R V O, named return value optimization, the caller hands over the address of b's slot. Then t is built right there, and there's nothing to move. A returned temporary is plain R V O.
Your turn. Two locals, and a flag picks which one returns. Can both be built in the caller's slot? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `T pick(bool c)` returns local x or y by flag. What runs?

scenes.head: Two objects, one slot
scenes.say: A move runs. Two different objects can't both live in one slot, so no N R V O. But a returned local still moves, never copies. Here pick prints move.

scenes.head: Guaranteed versus allowed
scenes.say: Since C plus plus seventeen, returning a temporary is guaranteed elided. So f compiles, even for a type that can't move. N R V O is only allowed, so g fails. And return s t d move of a local blocks it.

scenes.title: Why did print(10) compile?
scenes.statement: A function takes an Array. Calling it with the plain number ten silently builds an Array. Make that an error.
scenes.say: Here's a small surprise. A function takes an Array. For example, print of ten compiles, and builds an Array. We want both lines to fail.

scenes.head: Implicit, then explicit
scenes.say: A constructor with one argument is also a conversion. On the left, print of ten compiles, and so does a equals five. Both build a temporary array. Mark it explicit on the right, and both fail. Array b with parentheses still works.

panels.label: implicit
explicit

scenes.say: Your turn. With explicit on, one of these four lines still compiles. Which one? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: With `explicit Array(int)`, which line still compiles?

scenes.head: You already use both
scenes.say: Parentheses, since they name the type. The library uses both kinds. A string from a literal is implicit, a natural conversion. A vector from an int is explicit: a size is not a value. Unique pointer from a raw pointer is explicit: ownership stays visible. Default to explicit.
rows: error: explicit, a size isn't a value

scenes.head: Three constructors: which one runs?
scenes.say: Three constructors. Default takes nothing, parameterized takes values, copy takes a const reference. A is default, B seven, C copies B. This prints default, param seven, copy.

scenes.head: Destructors: when each one runs
scenes.say: Destructors? Locals at the brace, reversed. Heap objects at delete. Temporaries at the semicolon. Globals and statics after main returns. After an exception? Unwinding destroys the locals.
rows: locals at the brace, reversed; heap at `delete`

scenes.head: Virtual constructor? No, and why
scenes.say: Can a constructor be virtual? No, no object, no v pointer yet. Base builds first. So this prints Base. Need the effect? A virtual clone. Destructors should be virtual.

scenes.head: Move constructor: what it steals
scenes.say: What is a move constructor? It steals the pointers. Why noexcept? Otherwise vector copies on growth. Generated? Only if you declare no copy, move, or destructor.
rows: only if no copy, move, or destructor is declared

scenes.head: Copy versus move: cost and state
scenes.say: Copy versus move? Copy is O of n. Move is O of one. After a move, the source is valid but unspecified, here empty. Moving a const object copies.
rows: copy duplicates, O(n); move transfers, O(1)

scenes.head: std::move: a cast, nothing else
scenes.say: What does s t d move do? A cast to an rvalue reference. Nothing runs by itself. The move constructor steals, so here s is empty.

scenes.head: Lvalues and rvalues: which side
scenes.say: Lvalues and rvalues? An lvalue has a name and an address. An rvalue is a temporary, or a std move cast. A named rvalue reference is itself an lvalue.
rows: lvalue: has a name and an address
a temporary, or a cast by `std::move`

scenes.head: Perfect forwarding: keep the category
scenes.say: Perfect forwarding? Pass an argument on with its category intact. It needs a forwarding reference and std forward. It powers make unique and emplace back.
rows: lvalues stay lvalues, rvalues stay rvalues

scenes.head: Copy elision: no copy, no move
scenes.say: Copy elision? The compiler builds the result in the caller's slot. No copy, no move. Since C plus plus seventeen, a returned temporary is guaranteed. Here it prints ctor once. Named locals are optional.

scenes.head: explicit: stop silent conversions
scenes.say: Explicit versus implicit? A one argument constructor is a silent conversion. Explicit forbids that. Direct initialization and explicit casts still work. Prefer explicit, unless the conversion is natural, like string.
rows: direct-init or explicit cast, never implicit

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Do these next. One: a class that prints in all five special members. Two: a Buffer move constructor, and watch vector copy until noexcept. Three: a forwarding wrapper. Count copies with and without forward.
rows: predict every print before you run it
watch vector stop copying on growth

scenes.say: So say this. A move steals the pointers. The source is valid but unspecified, here empty. S t d move is a cast. Nothing runs. Return by name, and elision beats moving.
lines: Return by name. Elision beats moving.
